name: Sumariup
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 8 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Bruce, Leslie P., Jr. 1979. A grammar of Alamblak (Papua New Guinea). PhD thesis, Australian National University, Canberra. xii+561 pp. Chapter X 'The relationship of Alamblak to other Middle Sepik languages', pp. 472-533 (Glottolog ref 701032; hdl 1885/12495).
catalog_locator: Chapter X, section D 'The Sepik Hill languages', c. 'Morphological change' (isoglosses of short vs long forms), p.513 footnote 1, immediately before Table 137 'Isoglosses of Long and Short Forms' (p.514)
catalog_quote: Lewis and Lewis (1970) indicate that stress occurs on the first syllable of the word in Sanio-Hiowe. Stress typically occurs on the penultima in Sumariup and Alamblak, however, which may explain the retention of final syllables in those languages. Dye and Dye (1969) give evidence for phonemic tone-stress in Bahinemo. Thus tone-stress must be specified for each word in Bahinemo and may occur on any syllable in the word.

new_statements.citation: Bruce, Leslie P. 1979. A grammar of Alamblak (Papua New Guinea). PhD thesis, Australian National University. xii+561 pp. (hdl 1885/12495) [Appendix: the Sepik Hill languages, lexicostatistics, sound correspondences, isoglosses, pp. 472-545]
new_statements.locator: Appendix (the Sepik Hill languages), section c 'Morphological change', footnote 1, printed p. 513 (p. 524 of the ANU scan; lines 28542-28548 of). The footnote hangs on the sentence 'a regular phonetic conditioning in terms of stress-pitch patterns may turn out to be the explanation for the loss of particular syllables'. Table 137 'Isoglosses of long and short forms' (p. 514, p. 525) gives Sumariup forms with stress marks, e.g. [f'e§] 'pig'. text is letter-spaced and reads 'orl the penultima' and 'flnal' (scanned for 'on', 'final'); quote given de-spaced with those two characters corrected.
new_statements.relation_note: States that stress typically falls on the penult in Sumariup (and Alamblak), versus word-initial stress in Sanio-Hiowe and phonemic tone-stress on any syllable in Bahinemo; the body text speculates that stress-pitch patterns condition final-syllable loss across the family. Elsewhere the thesis has only segmental Sumariup material (barred-i correspondence ch. II, p. 116; sound-correspondence tables pp. 487-493; lexicostatistics Sumariup-Alamblak 59.9%). No tone claim for Sumariup.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress in Sumariup typically falls on the penultimate syllable (stated jointly for Sumariup and Alamblak, in contrast to initial stress in Sanio-Hiowe and lexical tone-stress in Bahinemo).
new_statements.exceptions: none listed; the claim is hedged with 'typically'
new_statements.identity_note: The sentence names Sumariup explicitly, contrasted with Sanio-Hiowe and Bahinemo; Bruce's Sumariup data are first-hand ('More extensive data were obtained by the author on a field trip in 1976 for Sumariup, Alamblak, Bahinemo.. three days of elicitation were spent for each language, collecting approximately 550 lexical items and 70 grammatical morphemes', pp. 24-25) plus the Dye/Townsend survey list. Same Sumariup = Latoma [siv]; Glottolog's suma1269 classification note cites this appendix (Bruce 1979: 472-519). Our bibliography lists the thesis for suma1269 as 'read: silent on stress' -- that reading is wrong: the ANU text is letter-spaced ('stre s s', 'S umar i up'), so the earlier keyword search returned 0 hits and the footnote on p. 513 was never seen. | Bruce's own 1976 Sumariup field data (Latoma village, upper Karawari; cf. PARADISEC Bruce collection already listed in round 1); Sepik Hill Family, eastern subgroup with Alamblak; no namesake issue [name in source: Sumariup (Sum.); pages 472-519 (cognate tables, Table 137); p.513 fn.1 (pdf page 524)]

sources.note: Nothing on Sumariup stress. Sumariup data = Dye et al. survey list plus Bruce's own 1976 3-day elicitation (~550 items, p.24-25); one segmental remark (Alamblak close transition corresponds to [barred-i] in Sumariup, ch.II); Appendix pp.472-519 gives lexicostatistics (Sumariup-Alamblak 59.9%) and segmental sound-correspondence tables (Table 136, Sumariup row) -- zero hits for stress/accent/tone in the appendix; rendered pp.489, 497 confirm segmental content only.
